newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Pik Botha says police lied to cabinet.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Pik Botha says police lied to cabinet.

text.p: Former South African foreign minister Pik Botha sought on Wednesday to distance the apartheid-era cabinet from the actions of its secret police, saying the police often lied to ministers.

Botha made the remarks in a statement to the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission in which he rejected charges that he had misled Botswana about a car bomb that South African agents planted in Gaborone 10 years ago.

His statement followed a spate of evidence to the commission and to courts conducting criminal trials in which former security police officers have said they believed their actions were either ordered or condoned by the cabinet.

Former security policeman Jack Cronje told the commission on Tuesday that he had been involved in rigging the bomb that was intended to kill a member of the African National Congress (ANC) in neighbouring Botswana.
The bomb, which exploded in April 1987, missed its intended target and killed a woman and two children.
Botswana protested to South Africa at the time but Botha's foreign affairs department responded that the explosion had been caused by an ANC guerrilla.

Cronje, who is applying to the truth commission for amnesty for his actions during the apartheid years, said on Tuesday that Botha must have known all along that South African agents set off the bomb.
But in a statement sent to the commission on Wednesday, Botha -- who retired from the cabinet last year -- said he objected strongly to Cronje's "unsubstantiated" statements.
He said his department had obtained its version of the car bomb explosion from the police.

"It's obvious that Cronje and his colleagues supplied false information to the deparment of foreign affairs... The cabinet was often deceived by certain members of the police dealing with these matters," Botha said.
"I consider Cronje's allegations as a disgraceful attempt to draw attention away from his irresponsible activities," he said.

F.W. de Klerk, leader of the National Party which introduced apartheid and one of only two former white presidents still living, has told the commission that he never ordered human rights abuses but that some appeared to have been carried out by rogue members of the security forces.
